stops.name: Kesswil, the parsonage on Lake Constance
stops.campa: In the parsonage at Kesswil, on the flat shore of Lake Constance, the pastor's wife Emilie Preiswerk bears a son to Johann Paul Achilles Jung. The child is named Carl Gustav after his grandfather, the Basel physician whom the city holds to be a natural son of Goethe: the legend the family carries like a sealed letter. The lake lies enormous before the house; his first memory will be of sun glittering through leaves, and of that inconceivable water. The House of Jung receives its rememberer.

stops.name: Schloss Laufen, the parsonage above the Rhine Falls
stops.campa: The family moves to the castle-parsonage of Laufen, perched directly over the Rhine falls. The cataract roars day and night beneath the child's window. Fishermen drown in the river; corpses are recovered on the rocks; black-coated men carry long boxes into the churchyard while his father speaks in a resounding voice at the graveside. The boy learns that Lord Jesus takes people to himself, and begins to distrust the taking. The falls become the ground-bass of his childhood, the sound under everything.

stops.name: Laufen, the underground temple and the man-eater
stops.campa: Aged between three and four, the boy dreams the first great dream of his life. In the meadow by the vicarage a stone-lined hole opens; a stair leads down to a doorway hung with green brocade. Beyond it, a red carpet runs to a golden throne, and on the throne stands an enormous phallus of naked flesh, twelve or fifteen feet high, a single eye gazing motionless upward from its rounded head. His mother's voice cries out above him in the dark. The subterranean god has shown himself first; the dream will haunt him for fifty years.
stops.quote: Yes, just look at him. That is the man-eater!
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 1 (the mother's voice in the dream)

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the parsonage by the Rhine
stops.campa: Pastor Jung is called to Klein-Hüningen, the fishing village at Basel's edge where the Wiese meets the Rhine. The family occupies the eighteenth-century parsonage with its great garden, its washhouse, its attic. Here the boy grows among peasant children, barges, floods, and the bones of the village churchyard. His mother by day is kindly and stout; by night, he perceives, she is uncanny: a priestess of the bear-cave, speaking with a second voice that says true things. The two atmospheres of his life, day and night, take up residence.

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the fire in the stones
stops.campa: In the garden wall before the parsonage the boy keeps a fire burning in a cave of the old stones: a fire that must burn forever, which he alone may tend; other children may feed only profane fires. Nearby juts his stone, the slope-set block on which he sits for hours playing the game of the exchanged question: he is sitting on the stone, but the stone may equally be saying 'he' of him. Thirty years later the question will be answered in masonry at Bollingen. The stone has already claimed him.
stops.quote: Am I the one who is sitting on the stone, or am I the stone on which he is sitting?

stops.name: Klein-Hüningen, the manikin in the attic beam
stops.campa: Toward the end of his tenth year the boy carves a little man with frock coat, top hat and shining boots, saws him from his ruler, and lays him in the pencil-case on a bed of wool with a smooth black Rhine stone painted into upper and lower halves: the manikin's own stone. He hides the case on the forbidden beam in the attic and visits it in secret, slipping in tiny scrolls written in a private script. No one can discover it; no one can destroy it. It is the first secret, the first god in the roof, and the torment of being divided against himself is gone.
stops.quote: The possession of a secret had a very powerful formative influence on my character; I consider it the essential factor of my boyhood.

stops.name: Basel, the Gymnasium am Münsterplatz
stops.campa: The country pastor's son walks daily into Basel to the Gymnasium beside the cathedral, among the sons of patricians who ride in carriages and speak of the Alps and the sea. For the first time he knows that his family is poor, that his boots are broken. Yet he carries the other knowledge too: that within him lives a second personality, an old man of the eighteenth century, buckled shoes and white wig, dignified and near to God, beside the schoolboy. Number One and Number Two begin their long negotiation on this square.

stops.name: Basel Münster, the cathedral vision
stops.campa: On a fine summer day the boy comes out of school onto the square and sees the cathedral roof glittering, new-tiled, under a blue sky, and thinks: the world is beautiful, and God made it and sits above it on a golden throne, and there the thought chokes. For three days and two nights he fights the forbidden conclusion, certain it means eternal damnation. Then he understands that God himself demands the sin of thinking it, as He demanded disobedience of Adam, and he lets the thought come. Grace descends on the Münsterplatz like weather. He has thought God to the end and lived.
stops.quote: God sits on His golden throne, high above the world — and from under the throne an enormous turd falls upon the sparkling new roof, shatters it, and breaks the walls of the cathedral asunder.

stops.name: Basel, the fainting spells conquered
stops.campa: A boy knocks him down on the cathedral square; his head strikes a curbstone. In the half-second of falling comes the thought: now you won't have to go to school any more. For six months the fainting spells excuse him from lessons, until he overhears his father confide to a visitor that the doctors fear epilepsy, that the boy may never earn his living. Struck as by lightning, he goes to his father's study, takes up his Latin grammar, and faints three times over it, and works on through each attack until the spells never return. He has met the neurosis and learned what it is.
stops.quote: Why, then, I must get to work!

stops.name: University of Basel, matriculation
stops.campa: Jung matriculates in medicine at the University of Basel, where his grandfather Carl Gustav the elder, Goethe's son, as Basel whispers and this register affirms, once held the chair and rebuilt the anatomy. In the Zofingia fraternity the young man lectures on the border zones of exact science, on the soul as something real, scandalous among materialists. Nietzsche's ghost still walks these streets and Bachofen in the flesh; Jung reads Kant, Schopenhauer, and the spiritualists by night. The grandfather's double inheritance, scalpel and Faust, is taken up.

stops.name: Basel, the séances with Helene Preiswerk
stops.campa: In the Preiswerk household his fifteen-year-old cousin Helly falls into trance at the table. Dead grandfather Samuel Preiswerk, the Hebraist who kept a chair for the spirits, speaks through her; she becomes Ivenes, a wise woman who travels among the stars and unrolls the family's past lives. For four years Jung attends the Saturday sittings, recording everything: the somnambulisms, the invented cosmology drawn in circles, the splinter-personalities forming and dissolving. Around the table the psyche shows him plainly that it is not one but many, and that the many want to become one.

stops.name: Basel, the father dies
stops.campa: Pastor Paul Jung dies in the Klein-Hüningen parsonage, broken on the faith he could not feel, having told his son only: believe, do not think. Carl, twenty, holds the dying man's head. Afterwards his mother speaks with her night voice, the second voice that is never wrong. The son inherits the unfinished religious question as other men inherit debts, and will pay on it for sixty-five years, down to a book called Answer to Job. The family moves; Carl becomes head of the house on a subsistence of borrowed francs and fossil-selling.
stops.quote: He died in time for you.
stops.quote_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 3 (the mother's No. 2 voice)
